reading.body:
Government AI activity is now a matter of public record: federal agencies disclose what they run, GAO audits those inventories, and 2,425 state AI bills are tracked to their source.

The pattern is layered oversight. GAO reviews federal AI inventories and management, state legislation is tracked bill by bill, and international indexes from Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, and Stanford HAI compare national readiness, strategies, and policy execution. This makes government AI adoption measurable and auditable, which shapes where and how public-sector systems can operate.

What this record does not show is the physical layer. The Oxford Insights index scores infrastructure as one dimension, but no scores or infrastructure findings appear here. The data covers governance, law, and policy, not the compute, buildings, or power behind the systems being governed.

summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The clearest measured picture of government AI use comes from GAO's audit of federal agencies. Twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, described as specific challenges or opportunities that AI may solve, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of those reported use cases were in the planning phase and not yet in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported that they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases. GAO also found the underlying data unreliable: five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their reported use cases while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, and two inventories included AI uses that the agencies later determined were not AI at all.

The uses GAO documented are operational rather than conversational. Agency reported uses included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting of scientific specimens for planetary rovers. GAO added that some agencies are using AI operationally to identify information security threats and to facilitate the review of large datasets. The most visible public-facing deployment in this material is America.gov, launched September 29, 2026 by the General Services Administration and the National Design Studio under an executive order. It answers questions in plain language drawn from about 29,000 government websites, running on Google Gemini and xAI Grok, with Phase 1 finding information and Phase 2, planned for 2027 with Login.gov, intended to handle applications and renewals. It offers no public API and its terms bar automated agents, so this site tracks it as a deployment rather than a source.

Money and vendor concentration show up in a few specific places. GAO notes that the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. On implementation, Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA established the AI Center of Excellence, both cited by GAO as full implementation of selected requirements. The America.gov fact sheet sets the scope of what gets folded into a single entry point: covered services are public-facing federal services that serve more than 100,000 users in a 12-month period and can be accessed or applied for online, with tax filing services provided by the Internal Revenue Service and national-security-sensitive services provided by the Department of War and the Intelligence Community excluded. The order directs the Administrator of General Services, the Administrator of the National Design Studio, and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to establish and operate America.gov and to integrate Login.gov with it.

Compliance is where the sources are most pointed. GAO found that federal law and guidance set several requirements for agencies implementing AI but they have not all been met, and that there is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, which means agencies cannot consistently manage AI and cannot effectively address AI risks and benefits until all requirements are met. Ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. OMB had not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, OPM had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, and OSTP did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements. GAO's conclusion is that without accurate inventories, the government's management of its use of AI will be hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data.

The international and policy layer is tracked by other organizations in this material. OECD.AI, the OECD Artificial Intelligence Policy Observatory, helps countries shape trustworthy AI with the OECD AI Principles and gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI, and a blog about AI policy, and it notes that organisations developing advanced AI systems can participate by submitting a report, which facilitates transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures. The GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand to create an integrated partnership. Oxford Insights describes its work helping governments increase the impact of their public services by empowering teams and harnessing technology, and its Government AI Readiness Index scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption. Stanford HAI's AI Index carries the government and policy track, including legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and this site tracks all state AI legislation, 2,425 bills, alongside the federal register.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to safeguards and inventory discipline before scale. GAO states plainly that AI poses risks that can negatively impact individuals, groups, organizations, communities, and society, and that given the rapid growth in capabilities and widespread adoption, the federal government should have safeguards to manage AI's complexities, risks, and societal consequences. The practical lesson from the audit is that most reported use cases were still in planning, that a minority were actually in production, and that the reporting itself was often incomplete, so an organization that cannot say precisely what it is running and at what life cycle stage is in the same position GAO criticized. The America.gov example shows the other direction, a single high-traffic entry point with named commercial models behind it and a phased plan that starts with answering questions before it touches transactions.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI describes itself as a policy observatory that helps countries shape trustworthy AI in line with the OECD AI Principles, and says it offers access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog on AI policy. It invites organisations developing advanced AI systems to take part by submitting a report, saying that sharing information would help make risk mitigation measures more transparent and comparable. The observatory states that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI combined under the GPAI brand into one integrated partnership. Its stated purpose is to help AI actors build and use systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
